To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Concentrations of nutrients (N, P, K) in floodwater and rice leaves are often low, but not as low as in oligotrophic lakes and in many soils.

(1) nutrient concentrations in the floodwater were often similar to those in oligotrophic lakes but were 4–45 lower for K and 15-90 times lower for N than those found in most soil solutions; (2) there were no significant differences in N, P or K concentrations between the three cultivars; and (3) there were no nutrient deficiencies for N, P or for K in the rice leaves at any of the four sites.
concentrations of nutrients in floodwater were similar to or higher than those found in most soil solutions but were much less than in the floodwater of most oligotrophic lakes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
nutrient uptake and transport processes in rice fields at water depths up 2m.
the nutrient status of floating rice and its environment.
the role of water in rice cultivation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
nutrient concentrations are generally low and that there may be some nutrient deficiencies in floating rice at water depths of up to 2 m.
nutrient concentrations in floodwater and rice are not limiting for rice growth at water depths of 0.5 to 2.0m.
there is no evidence of nutrient deficiency for rice growing at 2m water depth in central Thailand.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nutrient concentrations in floodwater and leaves of rice plants are not limiting to growth and yield of the rice crop in the areas studied.
the concentrations of N, P, and K in flood water are often sufficient for floating rice growth but that N may be deficient at the deeper sites.
nutrient concentrations in floodwater are generally low but not limiting to floating rice growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the concentrations of nutrients in the floodwater in these rice fields are often lower than those in most soil solutions, and that the concentrations of P and N in the leaves of rice growing in these fields are not necessarily a good indicator of the availability of these nutrients.
rice grown in flooded fields can take up nutrients from the water column.
the floodwaters of the central Thai floodplain are not particularly nutrient-rich.
